title: The Idea that Refused to Die (Part 2: The Schema Resurgence)
author: Dynamic Learning
summary: This Dynamic Learning post, the second in a series on schema theory, traces how the concept survived the mid-twentieth-century behaviourist era in the work of researchers who weren't explicitly studying schemas at all - Tolman's cognitive maps in rats, Tulving's finding that categorized lists improve recall, Bower's hierarchical-structure studies, and Miller's chunking research - before schema theory openly resurfaced in the 1970s. The piece uses Bransford and Johnson's well-known 'instructions for washing clothes' experiment to show that comprehension isn't about the text changing, but about whether the reader has the right prior schema activated to organize it, directly echoing Bartlett's original insistence that schemas are dynamic reconstructions rather than passive storage. It follows the parallel track of computer scientists like Marvin Minsky, whose 'frames' attempted to formalize Bartlett's intentionally loose concept into something precise enough for artificial intelligence, including default-assumption gap-filling that the author notes AI chatbots still get wrong today. The piece credits Rumelhart's work on story schemas and Anderson's application of schema theory to education with pulling the concept into classroom use, and closes on an ironic note: the same cognitive architecture that learning science spent decades rehabilitating may now be undermined by AI use that outsources the very processes schemas depend on to form and reorganize.
points: The piece traces how schema theory survived the behaviourist era underground, through Tolman's mental maps, Tulving's category-cued recall, Bower's hierarchical-recall findings, and Miller's chunking research, before formally resurfacing in the 1970s.
Bransford and Johnson's 'washing clothes' experiment is used to show that comprehension depends on activating the right prior schema, not on any change in the text itself.

Marvin Minsky's computational 'frames' are presented as an attempt to formalize Bartlett's deliberately loose schema concept into something precise enough for AI systems, including the default-assumption gap-filling that the author notes 'many AI chatbots today still do this, and often get it wrong.'

The essay closes with an explicit irony: the same schema theory that shaped modern learning design is now arguably being undermined by AI use, which outsources the cognitive work schemas depend on to form and reorganize.
quotes: Gordon Bower concluded in 1969 that when items in a to-be-remembered list are structured hierarchically, recall increases, adding weight to the notion that we unconsciously organise information based on shared characteristics.

Bransford and Johnson barely mention Bartlett, but their conclusions remain very Bartlettian. It's not the information that has changed. It's the cognitive organisation that has altered, emphasising Bartlett's insistence that schemas are dynamic, rather than simply being a long-term storage device.

According to Minsky, frames contain slots that can be filled with information about a particular situation, but if information is missing, default assumptions can sometimes fill the gaps (many AI chatbots today still do this, and often get it wrong).

Readers then use pre-existing cognitive frameworks (schemas) to anticipate and interpret story plots. Schemas aren't simply things that are stored in long-term memory that interpret the present. They also act as prediction machines.

People naturally organise, summarise, and remember stories based on how they fit with these idealised structural templates. We therefore don't remember a story simply as a sequence of sentences. We actively reconstruct it.
Understanding a text or event means finding a conceptual schema that fits and accounts for the details of that specific input.
There's an irony here as well. The increased use of AI undoubtedly undermines and disrupts schema formation and reorganisation by outsourcing the elements crucial to their emergence and functioning.
